prompt.context: Our client is a large, multinational consumer products company with business in over 200 countries. Today, we are going to focus on its US business. Our client has been following US demographic trends and has found that low income households have been growing two times as quickly as other consumer segments. Low income is defined as families with income at the poverty level or below. Our client has always had a premium product strategy. It sells its products in grocery stores, convenience stores, mass retailers, etc. but its products are always priced at the high-end of their respective categories. It has never targeted the low income segment before and doesn't have a low income strategy, but given the growth of this segment, our client is considering entering the low income segment.
prompt.question: Our client has 3 questions for BCG: 1) Should it have a low income strategy? 2) If it should have a low income strategy, what are some tactics it should deploy? 3) What are some of the risks the client may face?

clarifying_info.q: Where do low income consumers primarily shop?
clarifying_info.a: Low income consumers purchase largely in smaller, local shops

clarifying_info.q: Are there any low income consumer behaviors around personal care products like shampoo?
clarifying_info.a: Low income consumers can't afford salons, but will indulge on shampoos

clarifying_info.q: How do low income consumers approach baby-related products?
clarifying_info.a: Low income consumers are willing to spend more on baby food to protect their children

clarifying_info.q: Are there generics competing with the client's cold medicine?
clarifying_info.a: There are valid generics that compete with our client's cold medicine

exhibits.title: Product Category Sales and Low Income Consumer Spend
exhibits.shows: A table showing four product categories (Shampoo, Cold Medicine, Diapers, Baby Food) with four metrics each: total category sales (US$M), client category sales (US$M), total LI consumer spend on category (US$M), and LI consumer spend on client (US$M). LI = Low Income.

exhibits.title: Package Size and Price Comparison: Client vs. Competitors
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the client's package size and price against the average package size and average price of top 5 competitors across four product categories (Shampoo, Cold Medicine, Diapers, Baby Food).

framework: Assess the low income segment opportunity: size, growth rate, and whether there is unmet demand
Evaluate which products are best suited for the low income segment by analyzing current LI spend on client vs. total LI category spend (share gap)
Analyze competitive dynamics: client pricing vs. competitors, package size differences, and barriers to purchase
Identify tactics to serve the low income segment: packaging, pricing, channel strategy
Assess risks: brand dilution, cannibalization, channel conflict, competitive response

questions.prompt: What would you like to know to help the client answer its questions? Interpret Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies the LI share gap (client's share of LI spend vs. its overall market share) as the key signal. Client overall market shares: Shampoo 25% (100/400), Cold Medicine 20% (50/250), Diapers 50% (150/300), Baby Food 33% (100/300). Client LI shares: Shampoo 33% (30/90), Cold Medicine 10% (7.5/75), Diapers 25% (25/100), Baby Food 30% (30/100). For Diapers, the client holds 50% overall but only 25% of LI spend - a large underperformance suggesting LI consumers want diapers but aren't buying from the client. Cold Medicine LI share (10%) is also well below overall share (20%) but is confounded by generic competition. Shampoo and Baby Food show LI shares roughly in line with or above overall share.

math.setup: Client overall market share vs. client share of LI spend for each category
steps: Shampoo: overall share = 100/400 = 25%; LI share = 30/90 = 33% - overperforming
Cold Medicine: overall share = 50/250 = 20%; LI share = 7.5/75 = 10% - underperforming (but generics compete)
Diapers: overall share = 150/300 = 50%; LI share = 25/100 = 25% - significantly underperforming
Baby Food: overall share = 100/300 = 33%; LI share = 30/100 = 30% - roughly in line
math.answer: Diapers shows the largest gap between overall share (50%) and LI share (25%), indicating the most significant low income opportunity. Cold Medicine underperforms but generic competition is a complicating factor.

questions.prompt: What else would you like to know about diapers and cold medicine to assess the opportunity? Then interpret Exhibit 2 for diapers.
questions.guidance: Strong answer focuses on why LI consumers are not buying the client's diapers despite apparent interest. From Exhibit 2: client's diaper pack is 40 units at $20 ($0.50/diaper) vs. competitors' 32 pack at $16 ($0.50/diaper) - price per diaper is the same, but the absolute upfront cost ($20 vs. $16) is higher, which is a barrier for cash-constrained LI consumers. The key insight is that LI consumers face liquidity constraints, not a price-per-unit problem. For cold medicine, generics are a factor and the client is not interested. Candidate should note the price premium on cold medicine ($6 vs. $3 - a 2x premium) and that generic substitution explains the low LI share.

math.setup: Price per unit comparison for diapers
steps: Absolute price difference: $20 - $16 = $4 more upfront for client
math.answer: Price per diaper is identical, but the client's larger pack requires $20 upfront vs. $16 for competitors. LI consumers face an absolute price barrier, not a unit-price problem.

questions.prompt: What tactics should the client deploy for a low income diaper strategy? Calculate the revenue opportunity.
questions.guidance: Key tactic: reduce package size from 40 to 20 diapers to bring absolute price to $10 (below competitors' $16), while maintaining $0.50/diaper price. Revenue opportunity: LI total diaper spend is $100M; client currently captures $25M (25% share). If client closes gap to its overall 50% share, it could capture $50M - an incremental $25M in LI diaper revenue. Channel strategy: distribute through smaller local shops where LI consumers shop.

math.setup: Calculate incremental revenue if client achieves 50% LI share in diapers (matching its overall market share)
steps: Current LI diaper spend captured by client: $25M
Target LI share = 50% (matching overall market share)
math.answer: Reducing pack size to 20 diapers at $10 (matching $0.50/diaper) could generate an incremental $25M in LI diaper revenue if share rises to 50%.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks the client may face in pursuing a low income strategy?

categories.name: Brand Risk
ideas: Premium brand perception may be diluted if associated with value/budget products
Existing premium customers may trade down if lower-priced SKUs are visible in mass retail

categories.name: Cannibalization
ideas: Smaller, cheaper packs may cannibalize existing premium pack sales
Existing customers may switch to the new LI SKU to save money

categories.name: Channel Conflict
ideas: Mainstream retail partners (grocery, mass) may object to exclusive products sold in local shops
Introducing lower-priced SKUs may pressure overall channel pricing

categories.name: Operational Complexity
ideas: New SKUs increase manufacturing and supply chain complexity
Local shop distribution requires a different logistics model than national retail

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: Competitors may reduce prices or introduce competing smaller packs
Generics could expand into diaper category if client raises awareness of LI segment

recommendation: The client should pursue a low income strategy, focusing specifically on diapers

The recommended tactic is to reduce pack size from 40 to 20 diapers, cutting the absolute price from $20 to $10 - below the $16 competitor average - while maintaining the same $0.50 per diaper price point
This could generate an incremental $25M in revenue by increasing LI diaper share from 25% to 50%, in line with the client's overall market share
The client should distribute through smaller, local shops where LI consumers primarily shop
risks: Cannibalization of existing premium diaper sales if LI packs appear in mainstream retail
Brand dilution risk if the premium brand is associated with budget-priced products
next_steps: Pilot the 20-pack diaper SKU in select local shop channels in a few markets
Monitor cannibalization rates in adjacent channels
Evaluate whether other categories (baby food) also warrant LI-targeted SKUs given strong LI spend data
